paragraphs.text: [?] which the Craftsman brought about in the fashioning of man, as we said before, [?] must be specially unravelled through the yearly reminders of the lost. To bear witness to the truth, we shall prove by clear reasoning and by the testimony of examples that divination was invented and perfected by the devil, so that through it the spirit, its thought stained by the hope of a fleeting happiness, might use perverse discernment to pervert wretched men entangled in endless calamities.

No one can be found who doubts that the four elements, fire, water, air and earth, are the first principles of created things. But these elements differ from one another; indeed, their powers are opposed. So the pagans are in error when they assign primacy to the elements and go further, regarding fire as the supreme god, as though the others drew their substance from its heat. They do not know that all the elements are joined together by their very opposition, and that they too have God as their maker. He created them and set each in its own place and order: whatever we grasp by mind or thought, and certainly whatever we see with our eyes, was composed through the divine partnership of his Word, with the bodies balanced in due measure throughout this whole universe.

The inhabitants of Egypt, who enjoy the benefits of the waters, worship water. They pray to water and venerate the waters with a superstitious round of vows. But in their rites, which they call mysteries, they add tragic deaths and the deadly struggles of a dreadful calamity: incest with a sister, adultery committed, and this crime punished by the harsh vengeance of the husband. Isis is the sister, Osiris the brother, Typhon the husband.

When Typhon discovered that his wife Isis had been corrupted by her brother's incestuous lusts, he killed Osiris, tore him limb from limb, and scattered the still-quivering limbs of the wretched body along all the banks of the river Nile. Isis rejected Typhon and, to bury her brother and husband, took as her companions her sister Nephthys and Anubis the hunter. This is why Anubis was given a dog's head: with the skill of a tracking dog he found the parts of the mangled body. When Osiris had been found in this way, Isis gave him burial.

These were indeed kings in Egypt, and tyrants too. But Osiris was just, apart from what he did with his sister, while Typhon was violent, unrestrained and arrogant; so the one is worshipped and the other shunned. This is the sum of the rites of Isis. In their inner sanctuaries they keep an image of Osiris buried, and they mourn it with yearly lamentations. They shave their heads, so that by disfiguring their own heads they may bewail the pitiable fate of their king. They beat their breasts, gash their arms and reopen the scars of old wounds, so that by yearly mourning the ruin of that deadly and pitiable murder may be born again in their minds. And when they have done this for a fixed number of days, they pretend to search for the remains of the mangled body, and when they have found them they rejoice, as if their grief were laid to rest.

O wretched and perishable mortality! To send funeral offerings to your kings year after year, you neglect the supreme God, who composed all things by the measured skill of his divine craftsmanship, and so you lose both your hope and your life. You are not corrected by the splendour of the light shown to you; you do not seek the marks of recovered freedom; you do not recognize the hope of the salvation restored to you; you do not repent of your past crimes and ask for pardon.

In vain do you think that this water you worship will ever help you. There is another water by which men are renewed and reborn. This water you worship year after year is dried up by another force when its channels run dry, or else the deadly blood of your king defiles it. But the water you despise is set aflame [?] and adorned with the majesty of the venerable Spirit, so that from it saving health may flow over the old scars of conscience for those who believe.

Yet these deaths and mourning rites are real deaths; they actually happened, and their remains survive to this day, for the tomb of Osiris is still in Egypt and the remains of his cremated body can be seen. Even so, their defenders want to add a natural explanation. They say that Osiris is the seed of the crops, Isis the earth, and Typhon heat. Ripened by heat, the crops are gathered to sustain human life, separated from their union with the earth, and sown again as winter approaches. So they claim that the death of Osiris is when the crops are stored away, and his finding is when the crops, conceived by the life-giving warmth of the earth, begin to be brought forth again in their yearly generation.

Suppose this is the true meaning of these rites. Suppose vows are paid to the deities for the sake of the crops. Why do you add incest? Why adultery? Why the ruin of a pitiable punishment? Why do your rites hold up an evil example to men who go astray and are simply eager to sin? Let the natural meaning you speak of be hidden in some other way. But why should something known to everyone need hiding at all? Why do you mourn the fruits of the earth and lament the growing seeds?

All these things were given by the divine generosity of the supreme God to sustain the human race. For this, thanks must be given to the supreme God; his bounty is not something to be mourned. Weep instead for your own error, and lament your error with mourning that is renewed every time. Do not seek out someone else's death in yearly rites; rather, year by year prepare consolation for your own deaths.

O wretched man! You rejoice at having found something or other, while through these rites you lose your soul year after year. You find nothing there but an image you set up yourself, something you will only seek or mourn again. Seek instead the hope of salvation, seek the beginning of light, seek what will commend you or restore you to the supreme God. And when you have found the true way of salvation, rejoice, and then, with free and lifted voice, cry out: "We have found! We rejoice together!" when, after your repentance, you have been set free from these calamities by the pardon of the supreme God.

The Phrygians who live at Pessinus, along the banks of the river Gallus, give earth primacy over the other elements and claim that it is the mother of all things. Then, so that they too might have a yearly order of rites, they consecrated with yearly mourning the love of a rich woman, their queen, who wished to take a tyrant's revenge on the scorn of the young man she loved. To satisfy the angry woman, or to find comfort for her in her remorse, they proclaimed that the youth they had buried a little before had come back to life. And since the woman's heart burned with the impatience of excessive love, they built temples to the dead youth. Then they required the priests they ordained to suffer what the angry woman had done to avenge the insult to her spurned beauty. So in yearly rites the procession of this funeral is arranged under the guise of honouring the earth, and while men are persuaded that they are worshipping the earth, they are venerating the end of a wretched death.

Here too, most sacred emperors, to hide this error they want these rites as well to have been composed according to a natural explanation. They say that the earth loves the crops, and that Attis is what springs from the crops; the punishment he suffered is what the reaper does with his sickle to the ripened crops. His death, they say, is when the gathered seeds are stored away; his life again is when the sown seeds are put back in the ground in their yearly turn.

I would like them to answer my question now: why have they joined the simple matter of seeds and crops to a funeral, to death, to scorn, to punishment, to love? Was there nothing else to be said? Was there nothing else for wretched mortals to do in giving thanks to the supreme God for the crops? To give thanks for the crops reborn you howl; to rejoice you beat your breast. Nor, even when you have seen the true explanation, have you ever repented of doing this. Instead you act so as to be taken up with yearly mourning, always fleeing life and seeking death.

Let them tell me: what good did it do the crops that their offspring should be sown [?] with yearly howling, that people should groan over the disasters of a laid-out corpse, all of which they say was composed according to a natural explanation? You weep and beat your breasts, and you hide your mourning behind another explanation. The farmer knows when to break the earth with the plough, when to commit grain to the furrows, when to gather the harvest ripened by the heat of the sun, and when to thresh the dried crops. This is the natural explanation; these are the true sacrifices, performed by men of sound mind in their yearly labour. This simplicity is what the Godhead seeks: that men should follow the ordered laws of the seasons in gathering the fruits. Why were fictions of a wretched death sought out for this order? Why is something that ought not to be hidden hidden by tears? So they must admit that these rites were composed not in honour of the crops but in honour of someone else's death.

As for their saying that the earth is the mother of all the gods, those who assign first place to this element are right: she truly is the mother of their gods. We do not deny or dispute it, since it is from her that they gather the material for their gods, which they always make of stone or of wood. Seas flow around the whole earth, and in turn it is enclosed and bound by the circle of the encircling Ocean. It is covered by the round height of the sky, blown upon by the winds and sprinkled by the rains, and it confesses its fear by the tremors of its constant shaking. Consider what awaits you who worship these things, when your gods betray their weakness to you by daily confession.

The Assyrians and some of the Africans hold that air has the leadership of the elements, and they worship it in an imagined figure. They have consecrated this same element under the name of Juno, or of the Virgin Venus, if virginity ever pleased Venus. And so that incest should not be missing here either, they say that Juno, Jupiter's sister, was made his wife. Moved by some kind of veneration or other, they have made this element effeminate. Is it because the air lies between sea and sky that they honour it with the effeminate voices of priests? Tell me:

Is this a deity, one that looks for a woman in a man, one that the chorus of its priests cannot serve except by making their faces effeminate, smoothing their skin and disgracing their manhood with women's adornment? In the temples themselves one can see, to the public's grief, pitiable mockeries: men submitting to what women submit to, and flaunting with boastful display this stain of an impure and shameless body. They make their crimes public and confess the vice of their polluted bodies with the utmost stain of pleasure. They dress their long-grown hair like women, and, clad in delicate garments, they can scarcely hold up their heads on their weary necks. Then, having thus made themselves strangers to manhood, and filled with the music of the pipes, they call upon their goddess, so that, filled with an unholy spirit, they may foretell the future, as it were, to foolish men. What monster is this, what portent? They deny that they are men, and they are not women. They want to be thought women, but their bodies, such as they are, declare otherwise.

We must also consider what sort of deity this is that delights in lodging in so impure a body, that clings to shameless limbs, that is appeased by bodily pollution and defilement. Blush, you wretches, [?]: God made you otherwise. When your band comes before the tribunal of God the Judge, you will bring back with you nothing that the God who made you can recognize. Cast off this error that brings such calamity, and at last abandon the pursuits of a profane mind. Do not condemn the body God made by the wicked law of the devil. Help yourselves in your calamities while time still allows. The mercy of God is rich, and he forgives gladly. Leaving the ninety-nine sheep, he seeks the one

that was lost; and when the prodigal son returns, the father gives him back his robe and prepares a feast. I do not want the multitude of your crimes to make you despair. Through his son [?] Christ our Lord, the supreme God sets free those who are willing and gladly forgives those who repent, and he does not demand much in order to forgive: by faith and repentance alone you can redeem whatever you lost through the wicked persuasions of the devil.

The Persians and all the Magi who live within the borders of the Persian lands give preference to fire and think it should be ranked above all the elements. They divide fire into two powers, assigning its nature to both sexes and representing the substance of fire by the image of a man and of a woman. The woman they depict with a triple face and entwine her with monstrous serpents. They do this so as not to depart in any way from their author, the devil, but so that their goddess, teeming with serpents, may be adorned with the spotted emblems of the devil.

The man, however, is a cattle-thief whom they worship, and they transfer his rites to the power of fire, as his prophet has handed down to us, saying: "Initiate of cattle-theft, right-hand son of a noble father." They call him Mithras, and they hand on his rites in hidden caves, so that, always plunged in the murky gloom of darkness, they may shun the grace of bright and serene light. O dreadful consecration of a deity! O monstrous inventions of a barbarous law, to be fled! You believe him to be a god whose crimes you confess. So you who say that in these temples, duly [?] by the rite of the Magi, in Persian fashion, why do you praise these things of the Persians alone? If you think it worthy of the Roman name that it should serve the rites of the Persians and the laws of the Persians [?] which is consecrated armed with a shield and covered with a breastplate [with sword and spear]. There is also a third part, which in the rough and secret places of forests and fields embraces the company of wild beasts.

The last part of this threefold division considers the ways of lust, which displays depraved desires and the drowsy cravings [?] in darkness. So they assign one part to the head, as of a man [?]; another seems in some way to belong to the kidneys [?]. Another they place in the heart, so that, like a forest, it may be seen to hold the variety of differing thoughts that we conceive with manifold intent. The third part is located in the liver, from which lust and pleasure are born. For there the gathered fertility of the generative seed stirs up the desire of craving with natural goads.

Look carefully, then, at what this division accomplishes, so that the reasoning of truth may easily overthrow the invention. The soul is divided; its substance is separated into different kinds of activity, and with its order dissolved it begins to be [no longer?] what it had been. For mind is one thing, anger another, lust another. This separation, then, dissolves the soul, and the soul suffers the greatest loss from this partition. Nor does a thing keep its form intact when it is separated and divided into three opposing parts; indeed, to speak more truly, it becomes mortal by that very division. For whatever can be divided is a body, and whatever is a body must be mortal. Therefore, if the soul is divided, it is a body; if it is a body, it must itself be mortal. A fine and splendid consequence of this error! This conclusion does us the greatest favour: through the inventions of these trifles they would have souls be mortal.

Such, most sacred emperors, are the elements that lost men have consecrated. But other superstitions still remain whose secrets must be laid open: those of Liber and Libera. All of these must be specially made known to your sacred minds, so that you may know that in these profane religions too it is the deaths of men that have been consecrated. Liber, then, was the son of Jupiter, that is, of a king of Crete. Since he had been born of an adulterous mother, he was brought up in his father's house with more care than was fitting. Jupiter's wife, whose name was Juno, was stirred by the fury of a stepmother's heart and laid plots of every kind to kill the infant.

When the father was setting out on a journey abroad, knowing his wife's silent resentment, he entrusted the protection of his son to guardians who seemed to him suitable, so that the angry woman might not do anything by treachery. Then Juno, finding a favourable moment for her plot, and inflamed all the more because the father, on setting out, had handed the boy the throne and sceptre of the kingdom, first bribed the guardians with royal rewards and gifts. Next she placed her henchmen, who were called the Titans, in the inner parts of the palace, and with rattles and a skilfully made mirror she so enticed the boy's childish mind that, drawn by a child's desire, he left the royal throne and was led to the place of ambush.

There he was seized and slaughtered, and so that no trace of the murder could be found, the band of henchmen cut his limbs into pieces and shared them out among themselves. Then, to add another crime to this crime, because they greatly feared the tyrant's cruelty, they cooked the boy's limbs in various ways and ate them, feasting on a human corpse in a banquet unheard of until that day. His sister, whose name was Minerva and who was herself a party to the crime, kept the heart she had been allotted, both as clear evidence for her accusation and so that she might have something with which to soften her father's furious onslaught. When Jupiter returned, his daughter set out the course of the crime.

Then the father, shaken by the deadly calamity of this disaster and the cruelty of his bitter grief, tortured the Titans in various ways and killed them. In avenging his son he omitted no torment or punishment, but raging through every kind of penalty he avenged the death of his son, such as he was, with a father's feeling but with a tyrant's power. Then, since the father could no longer bear the torments of his grieving heart, and since the pain of his bereavement was softened by no consolation, he had a statue of the boy made of moulded gypsum. He placed the boy's heart, by which the crime had been discovered when his sister reported it, in that part of the figure where the outline of the chest had been shaped. After this, instead of a tomb he built a temple and appointed the boy's tutor as priest. His name was Silenus.

To soften the savagery of the raging tyrant, the Cretans established festival days of mourning and arranged a yearly rite with a triennial consecration, doing in order everything that the boy did or suffered as he died. They tear a live bull with their teeth, recalling the cruel banquet in yearly commemorations, and wailing with discordant cries through the secret places of the forests they feign the madness of a raging mind, so that the crime might be believed to have been done not by treachery but in madness. The chest in which the sister had secretly hidden the heart is carried in front, and with the music of pipes and the clash of cymbals they imitate the rattles with which the boy was deceived. Thus, to honour a tyrant, a servile populace made a god of one who could not even have a burial.

There was also another Liber, a tyrant at Thebes, conspicuous for his power in the magic arts. Having taken possession of women's minds with certain drugs and spells, he ordered these frenzied women to commit cruel crimes at his whim, so that he had noblewomen, their minds captured, as servants of his lusts and his crimes. What crimes he committed, and what outrage he commanded a mother to commit against her son or sisters against their brother, is recounted daily on the stage by the authors of tragic poetry, so that the criminal cruelty of that wicked tyrant is always born again in the minds of the audience through these deadly tales.

Lycurgus, protected by a sober alliance of men, stripped him of his kingdom and drove him from his country; for an effeminate man could not long withstand the united will of men. It is sung in the gymnasia of the Greeks that he was effeminate and served the lusts of his lovers. Nor was Lycurgus content with his flight and exile. Fearing that if he fled and was received by others he might plant the shameful seeds of his crimes in another land as well, Lycurgus girded on his sword and pursued this disgrace to his country with a threatening edict. Then Liber, throwing away the fillets that he bound with circlets of vine-leaf garlands, fled with his half-male retinue — for only the partners of his debaucheries, outrages and lusts followed him — and wandered in great fear and despair along all the shores of the neighbouring sea. There,

among drunken girls and wine-sodden old men, while the procession of his crimes still went before him — one hideous in black clothing, another terrifying with a snake held up, another with bloody mouth as he tore apart the live limbs of a beast — he was caught by Lycurgus and thrown into the sea from a nearby cliff, which formed a vast precipice of impassable rocks. This was so that his mangled body, long tossed by the sea waves, might by this stern punishment recall the minds of straying peoples to the order of sanity and sobriety. Homer describes this end of Liber, to expose his flight and terror and to show his death, saying: "...struck with an ox-goad; and Dionysus, terrified, plunged beneath the wave of the sea, and Thetis received him in her bosom, frightened, for a mighty trembling held him at the man's shout." http://data.perseus.org/citations/urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc1:6.116-6.155

Our consul Postumius too imitates you, Lycurgus. He follows your sober policy and does not stray from your wholesome laws. For, as we find in the books of annals, the crimes of the Bacchanalia were uncovered when a certain young man named Aebutius informed against them. At that time morals in the city of Rome were still sound, and no one, through loose living, hankered after foreign superstitions. Then the senate did not fail the consul, nor the laws of the state the senate, nor the consul the laws. Instead, all who were handing down the wicked inventions of this rite were tracked down, and against all of them a capital penalty was decreed by the decision of the council, after a severe, indeed a Roman, inquiry. Nor did the consul's avenging swords rest until this evil had been cut out by the roots. O punishment worthy of the Roman name! O praiseworthy constancy of ancient virtue! The consul was unwilling to spare even his own citizens when foreign vices were being corrected to purify the fatherland.

Following this contagion of rites, and copying the pattern of that funeral, is the death of a daughter consecrated by Ceres, a woman of Henna. For everything the father had done in Crete for his son, Ceres established at Henna after losing her daughter, unable to bear a mother's grief. I will touch briefly on how this came about. Ceres had an only daughter, whom the Greeks call Persephone and our people, with the word altered, Proserpina, and many men sought her in marriage. Her anxious mother was weighing the merits of each, and while the mother's decision still seemed uncertain to them all, a rich countryman, who was called Pluto because of his riches, carried off the girl, whom he had found near Percus. He was driven by a reckless heat of desire, could not endure the delays and postponements, and was burning with the fires of a perverse love. Percus is a lake within the territory of the city of Henna, very lovely and pleasant, and its loveliness comes from the variety of its flowers: all year round it is crowned with flowers that follow one after another.

There you will find every hyacinth swelling on its stalk; there the narcissus with its tuft, which paints a golden rose above; there white ivy creeps softly over the ground, and marjoram, sweetly blushing, is found beside purple violets; nor do white lilies fail that garland. It was a place perfectly suited both to entice girls' hearts with its charm and to hold them there. In this place Pluto found the maiden towards evening. She was seized by force, set upon his carriage and carried off, her clothes torn and her hair dishevelled. Nor did her trimmed nails avail anything against her rustic lover, nor did her shrieks and wailing help her, nor the clamour of the other girls.

Then, since no one came to help from the city, one of them, made swifter by her very fear, ran quickly and told the mother that the maiden had been carried off. The mother, enraged at the abductor, led an armed band against him. Nor did the woman's approach escape Pluto; when he turned his eyes back towards the city and saw countless troops coming with the mother, he took a deadly decision out of despair. He drove the four-horse team that drew the carriage into the middle of the lake, which was sunk in deep whirlpools. There he went down together with the maiden he loved, and presented the wretched mother with the deadly spectacle of her daughter's death.

So that the mother's grief might find some measure of comfort, the people of Henna invented the story that the king of the underworld had carried off the maiden; and so that belief might follow the fiction, they gave out that he had come up again with the maiden by another way, near Syracuse. They built a temple, indeed, to both the abductor and the maiden, at carefully collected expense, and decreed annual vows in the temple. But the mother's grief was not overcome by any means, nor were the torments of a woman's impatience healed. Truly believing that her daughter had been seen near Syracuse, she travelled by night, with her steward Triptolemus as guide, to the shore of the city of Syracuse, in mourning clothes and squalid neglect. Nor was there lacking there someone to deceive a mother ready to believe anything about her misfortunes: one Pandarus, whoever he was, said he had seen the abductor board a ship with the maiden not far from Pachynus. The woman was persuaded, and because she longed to hear that her daughter was alive in any condition whatever, she rewarded the city with countless gifts.

The Syracusans, spurred on by the woman's generosity, consecrated the maiden's abduction, and to soften the mother's grief they adorned the procession of a miserable funeral with the honour of temples. But even this was not enough for the mother: she boarded a ship and searched for her daughter along foreign shores. So, tossed by waves and storms, she came to a place in the city of Attica, and there, received as a guest, she distributed wheat, until then unknown to the inhabitants. The place took its name from the woman's homeland and from her arrival: it was called Eleusis, because Ceres had come there after leaving Henna.

Thus, because she had distributed the grain she had brought and taught the art of gathering crops, after her death, for the benefit that sprang from the abundance of crops, she was both buried in that place and consecrated, and called by a divine name together with her daughter. For the fickleness of the Greeks loves to give divine names to those who have conferred anything on them, or helped them by counsel or valour; and so they repay the favour of benefits by calling gods, and believing to be gods, those who have once been of use to them. So Nysa has no doubts about Liber, nor does Sparta hesitate about its new stars; mournful Oeta burns and consecrates Hercules, and the tomb of the dead Jupiter is still worshipped by the vain Cretans.

Yet, most sacred emperors, something more is added to swell this profane error, to defend these double-named figures, that is, Liber and Proserpina, with a kind of greater authority. For the inventions of the Greeks would refer Liber to the sun, while they make up the claim that Proserpina, whom they call Libera, is the moon. How absurd and how pitiful this is we can gather from the very reasoning of truth. Who has seen the sun as a boy? Who deceived him? Who killed him? Who tore him apart? Who divided him up? Who feasted on his limbs? Who carried off the moon? Who hid her away?

Who made her Pluto's wife? But they want to shield this error once more with a natural-philosophical explanation: they think that in this way they can venerate the undivided and the divided mind, that is, the undivided nous and the divided nous.

Tell me, wretched mortals, why do you add funerals to the things of nature? Why do you pollute God's ordering with the atrocity of cruel deaths? What need was there for so harsh and cruel a torment? What is the point of this belief, that the course of a deadly calamity should be joined to divine things, that the nature of the stars, which the supreme God made with fixed laws, should be linked with the mourning of mortal calamity? What purpose does what you do serve? You mix earthly with heavenly things, the perishable with the things above, the dark with the shining, consecrating the sorrows and mourning of human beings with divine honours.

If the whole human race were called together and the sun held an assembly and spoke, he might perhaps strike your desperate folly with a speech like this: "Who drove you, perishable men who rebel against the supreme God every day in various ways, to so great a crime that, in the profane error of a wicked desire, you say I die and live at your pleasure? If only the fictions of your mad thinking would proceed in the usual manner, or in a single fashion! If only the wickedness of your criminal thinking would run riot without insulting me! As it is, flinging yourselves over precipices, you do not spare me either, and your talk has no reverence at all; you hasten to your ruin and death to my disgrace. Some, in Egypt, in obstinate fury of mind, drown me in the waters of the Nile

and its swift whirlpools; others cut off their genitals and mourn me; others have me slain by a cruel death and either boil me in a pot or fix the mangled limbs of my body on seven spits. The one who flatters me a little with gentler speech invents the story that I am the charioteer of a four-horse chariot. Cast away at last the ruin of such great madness, and, addressed with saving counsel, seek the true way of salvation. Whoever either conceived or invented these things is an enemy of God; and no simple crime is his, nor does an ordinary punishment follow him who pollutes hidden things with profane beliefs and invents such tales about the glorious work of God.

Mourn your dead, you who will yourselves die a similar death; offer funeral sacrifices to your kings as you please, and soothe their bereavements with some other kind of remedy. Mourn Liber, mourn Proserpina, mourn Attis, mourn Osiris, but without insult to our dignity. I do not want you to drag me through their tombs and ashes; I do not want my name to supply fuel for your error. I was made by God for the beginning of the day; that alone is enough for me. Why do you strip me of the dignity of an honourable office? God made me one thing and ordered me to be one thing, and you divide me up as you like and tear me apart as your whim desires. Whatever I am, I simply obey, and I want you to understand nothing else about me than what you see. This is pleasing to God, this God gladly embraces, this leads people to the way of salvation: that you cast off your errors and drink in God's grace simply and faithfully."

Let it suffice, most sacred emperors, to have said this much by way of impersonation. But now, trained by instruction in the sacred readings, I address these lost men in the language of religion. If those you worship are gods, why do you mourn them? Why do you lament them with yearly mourning? If they deserve tears and mourning, why do you heap divine honour on them? So do one of two things: either do not mourn them, if they are gods; or, if you think them worthy of mourning and tears, do not call them gods, so that the majesty of the divine name is not polluted by your mourning and tears.

But since a lost mind, entangled in the snares of criminal desire, cannot be called back by any reasoning, I will go on to the rest, so that, once everything that profane wickedness has consecrated is made public and exposed, the mercy of God, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, may raise the fallen, call back to itself those who flee, strengthen the doubting, correct the straying, and, what matters most, give life to the dying.

In very many cities of the East, though this evil has crossed over to us as well, Adonis is mourned as the husband of Venus, and his slayer and his wound are shown to the bystanders. For Mars, changed into the appearance and form of a wild boar so as to claim first place in Venus' love for himself, struck the young man as he rushed heedlessly against him. If Adonis was a god, why did he not know of his rival's ambush? If a man, why was he contending with a superior?

But I hear that someone else shared Venus' marriage bed as well: Vulcan, unless I am mistaken, is said by these worshippers of the gods to be Venus' husband. What a laughable belief of vain men! The adulterer, set between two husbands, is caught by one and defeats the other. But look what body the adulterous god chose for himself in order to defeat a husband! He preferred to be a pig. If he had the power to change his body, he ought rather to have taken on the appearance and form of a lion. But those who know the natures of animals say that the lion, for all the ferocity of its wild spirit, preserves the virtue of chastity. Rightly, then, the adulterer scorned the form of a lion and chose that of a lustful animal.

Here let us now treat the mysteries of the gospel tradition. When the demon was cast out, the Lord gave it the herd of pigs, and not without reason: so that the unclean spirit, hurled together with lustful animals down steep cliffs and into the waves, might be seized by a fitting death through the various deaths of the pigs.

I hear that Cinyras of Cyprus gave a temple to a prostitute who was his mistress (her name was Venus), and also initiated a great many people into the rites of the Cyprian Venus and bound them over to vain consecrations; he also laid down that whoever wished to be initiated should, once the secret of Venus had been handed on to him, give the goddess one as by way of payment. What sort of secret this is we must all understand in silence, because its very foulness prevents us from explaining it more plainly. The lover Cinyras rightly followed the laws of prostitutes: he ordered that the consecrated Venus be given a fee by her priests, as if she were a harlot. Those who worship Sabazius, when they initiate someone, draw a snake, Jupiter, through his bosom. The vices of the first error still run riot: whatever destroyed mankind is worshipped, and the cunning and malicious cruelty of the deadly serpent is adored.

In the rites of the Corybantes, fratricide is worshipped. For one brother was killed by two, and so that no evidence might reveal the murder of a brother, he was consecrated by his fratricidal brothers at the foot of Mount Olympus. This same figure is worshipped by the foolish belief of the Macedonians: he is Cabirus, to whom the Thessalonians once made supplication with bloody mouths and bloody hands. So we must consider what sort of deity it is that fratricidal madness invented in order to conceal a fratricide.

Therefore whoever venerates these rites with devoted mind, whoever is pleased by the fearful contagion of this superstition, is either seeking comfort for his own wrongdoing or silently praising their crimes in his thoughts, wishing this, seeking this, above all greatly desiring this: that what was permitted to his gods may be permitted to him too, and that a likeness of morals may bring him into the fellowship of such a life.

Someone takes pleasure in adultery: he looks to Jupiter and from him gathers fuel for his desire. He approves, imitates and praises the fact that his god deceives as a swan, abducts as a bull, sports as a satyr, and, so that he may grow used to being generous in his vices, corrupted a royal maiden shut away by pouring out gold in abundance. Someone takes pleasure in the embraces of boys: let him look for Ganymede in Jupiter's bosom, let him see Hercules searching for Hylas with impatient love, let him learn of Apollo captured by desire for Hyacinthus; let one see Chrysippus, another Pelops, so that he may say that through his gods he is permitted whatever is today punished most severely by Roman law.

It is hard to list all their adulteries, who seduced Amymone, who Alope, who Melanippe, who Chione and Hippothoe; your god, of course, is recorded as having done these things. He whom they would have correct the sins of erring men by stern oracles loves Sterope, abducts Aethusa, violates Zeuxippe, pursues Prothoe, and flatters Arsinoe with adulterous desire. But out of that flock of seduced women one girl both escaped and defeated her divine lover: the god who divines and foretells the future could neither find Daphne nor violate her. Someone submits to being used as a woman and seeks comfort for his effeminate body:

let him see Liber repaying his lover, even after death, the promised reward of lust by imitating a shameful act of intercourse. If anyone, from a monstrous heat of desire, arms himself to murder his father, let him take his start from Jupiter; whoever longs for a brother's blood, let him follow the practice of the Corybantes; and let those who desire incest take their examples from Jupiter: he slept with his mother, married his sister, and, to complete the crime of incest, also approached his daughter with the intent of a seducer.

Someone pursues his inferiors with jealous gnashing of teeth and longs to torment his adversary with cruel ferocity: let him learn from Apollo, from what befell Marsyas, the agonies of cruel tortures. Someone desires another's property and tries to gain it by killing its owner: let him see how Hercules killed Geryon and drove off the Spanish cattle. If anyone delights in the indiscriminate slaughter of people, let him carefully study the perverse desires of Mars. The crowd of sinners gathers the seeds of almost every crime from its gods, and so that a lost mind may commit crime with impunity, it defends itself with greater authority from the precedents of crimes gone before.

If a seducer seeks the rewards of debauchery, if he wishes to learn the way of solicitation, let him see Jupiter's gold in the lap of a seduced woman. If a public traitor longs, out of wicked desire, to betray the guardianship of a kingdom entrusted to him, let him look to those who betrayed Saturn to his son. If anyone bent on wrongdoing asks how far the right of hospitality may be violated, or how far the laws of friendship may be overturned, or how far the sacred bond of the shared table may be outraged, see, let him learn the whole sequence of crimes from what befell Tantalus.

O grim comfort of criminal desire! O lamentable belief of men! O bloody study of unhappy imitation! You have made heaven into a stage and led erring minds over steep precipices to cruel disaster, since the way of crime is shown to people eager to sin by the examples of the gods. But in this law of crimes, in this confession of wickedness, let us give thanks to those who have also revealed to us, though we did not know it, the ruin and deaths of these gods, so that we might learn everything through so many who stood in the way [?]. For even among the ancients, although the venerable condescension of our Lord Christ had not yet shed light on the earth, there was a religious steadfastness in scorning superstitions.

Diomedes, chaste and sober, wounds Venus, defeats and strikes Mars. By the decree of Otus and Ephialtes, Mars, mighty in war, was condemned to temporary exile and bore iron chains. Jupiter mourns his son Sarpedon, dead at Troy, and Neptune does not receive from a proud king the wages for the walls he built. Apollo pastures another king's flocks, and someone else reports to the all-seeing Sun the deaths of his slaughtered cattle. Sparta buries the Castors, Hercules burns on Oeta, and Aesculapius is struck by lightning elsewhere. Vulcan, hurled down by his father, breaks his foot; Liber, fleeing Lycurgus, dies. Venus, caught in adultery, is exposed, and after marriage to a god pursues the bed of Anchises, a man. Saturn, fearing for his kingdom, devours his sons, and, fleeing his son, hides as a fugitive in Italy. Juno is scorned for love of Catamitus, the Moon comes down to Endymion, and Jupiter, bringing help to the Trojans against the will of his wife and daughter, is deceived and falls asleep.

O shameful confession! O [?] and lamentable worship! O pitiable condition of harsh slavery! The sacrilegious rule of tyrants dragged holy men, who believed with minds devoted to God, to the worship of these gods, and so that another crime might be added to this crime, death was decreed for those who refused. Move your temples to the theatre instead, so that the secrets of these religions may be handed down on the stage; and so that wickedness may leave nothing out, make actors your priests. No worthier place could be found for these religions. There let a vile crowd sing of the loves of the gods; there let their misfortunes and deaths be danced; there, better than in the temples of the gods, let impious and criminal teachers teach the lost mind adultery and crime.

Learn also, most holy emperors, the origin of the venerated deity of Alexandria, so that, once our common frailty has been laid bare, our discourse on mortality may be called back to the beginning of the truth. When in Egypt [?] as the crops withered, the malicious [?] of famine [?], the young man Joseph, born of the seed of a religious patriarch, interpreted the king's dream and revealed everything that was impending. Joseph was the son of Jacob; he had been sent to prison for his chastity, and after interpreting the dream he was released and became a sharer in the kingdom. For by gathering and storing the produce of seven years he relieved, with the foresight of a divinely inspired mind, the want of the following seven years.

After his death the Egyptians, following their nation's ancestral custom, built temples to him, and so that posterity might learn the grace of his just distribution, the measure with which he had distributed grain to the hungry was placed on his head. His name too, so that he might be worshipped with greater reverence, was taken from the first founder of his line. For since he was the great-grandson of Sarah, from whom Abraham, by God's favour, had received a child when she was ninety, he was called Serapis in Greek, that is, Sarras pais, "Sarah's child."

But this was done against Joseph's will, or rather after his death; for a religious mind dedicated to the supreme God could never have been brought to such a crime as himself to offer superstitious people the allurements of error from his own name, especially since he knew that it is written in God's most holy laws that no one should venerate or worship any such thing. He is worshipped in Egypt, he is adored there, a crowd of temple-wardens guards his image, and the erring people, in memory of antiquity, still today guard with contentious zeal the order of rites established in honour of a most upright and wise man.

But in this image too, as in the others, the unclean spirits of demons gather because of the constant sacrifices. For the victims, and the blood poured out by the constant slaughter of cattle, achieve nothing except that the substance of the demons, who are begotten by the devil's procreation, is nourished by that blood. Porphyry, the defender of idols, the enemy of God, the foe of truth, the master of criminal arts, has revealed this to us with clear proofs. For in the books he calls On the Philosophy from Oracles, while proclaiming its majesty he confessed its weakness. At the very beginning of the books, that is, at the very outset [?], he said: "Serapis, when summoned and brought into the body of a man, gave the following reply."

Now let these lost men tell me: which is the more powerful, the one who summons, commands and confines, or the one who is summoned and obeys, and who, when he has come, is confined in the body of the man who receives him by the power of the one who gives the order? We thank you, Porphyry, for your books: you have revealed to us the substance of your gods; we have learned from you how far your gods serve men at their command. Your Serapis is summoned by a man and comes, and when he has come he is at once confined on command, and the necessity of speaking is imposed on him, perhaps against his will.

So among us, when your gods begin to harm people, the scourges of religious speech chastise them; so your gods, lodged in human bodies, are tormented by the word of God with the fire of spiritual flames; and those who are worshipped as gods, among us, through the healing remedies of religious faith, by the grace of Christ, are made subject to human command, endure torments for all their resistance, and, defeated, are brought under avenging punishments.

I shall also try to explain who the Penates are, so that I may not seem to have left anything out. Those who think life is nothing but licence to eat and drink have shaped these gods for themselves out of the baseness of their own appetite, consecrating under this name, as if for the welfare of mankind, the nourishment of the body that is supplied by daily meals. Because the body's weakness is restored by meals, they decreed that food alone is god, not knowing the truth of the divine oracle. For when

the Lord Jesus Christ, concerned for our salvation, was contending with the devil in a struggle worthy of his divine majesty, in order to free from his jaws the humanity he bore, he shattered him with this reply. For when the devil said to him, "If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become bread," the Lord answered him, "Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God." So, knowing nothing of the true substance of the human race, they consecrated daily meals under this name: for everything that people eat is called penus, provisions; hence the cella penaria, the storeroom, and hence the Penates, gods devised by abject and grovelling men in their wretched imagination.

Learn, too, what Vesta is, so that you may not think her something ancient, or something discovered amid the utmost awe of religion. She is the household fire that serves daily needs on the hearth. So let her have cooks, and not wretched virgin priestesses, who, scorning the very embers of that fire, are either driven to sin by prostituting their bodies or, if they persist in virginity, lose the honourable dignity of a glorious name.

Hear also what the divinity of the Palladium is. It is an image made from the bones of Pelops, and Abaris the Scythian is said to have made it. Now consider what sort of thing it must be, consecrated by a barbarian Scythian. Is there anything among the Scythians put together by human reason? Could that savage race of men, always rampaging with cruel and inhuman ferocity, find anything right in establishing religions?

Abaris sold this image to the Trojans, promising empty things to foolish men. A god was sold so that it might profit its buyer, and the buyer humbly worshipped whatever he had seen put up for auction a little before. The substance of the image itself is the bones of Pelops. If you wish, Abaris, to make wretched men venerate human bones, at least gather the remains of a purer and chaster man, so that the idol you make may gain some merit from the virtues of a man. Pelops was the darling of a lover, and for a long time suffered the disgrace of prostituted modesty. Nor, when he was grown, did he lack crime: he killed the man whose daughter he was seeking by the treachery of a betrayer; then he assailed the betrayer himself with perjury and, so as not to pay the promised reward, hurled him down a sheer precipice. Behold the man whose bones were chosen to become a god that would protect cities and kingdoms!

But it never protected anything, nor was it of any use, and from the fortunes of the cities in which it stood it has seen what awaits it. Troy was burned by the Greeks, Rome by the Gauls, and from both fires the Palladium was saved—saved, however, not by its own powers but by human protection. For men rescued it from both places, and it was carried off so that it should not burn in a fire kindled by men. So great a divinity needed human protection, and sought human help so as not to burn! The Palladium was spared the fire, not freed from it: the sentence stands, the punishment remains, the fire threatens, the fire presses on, and it will not be able to escape it.

Already the heavenly flame is in labour, already the coming of divine punishment is shown, already the destruction of the disaster to come is announced. In this fire the Palladium will be unable to find a hiding place: that fire searches out what is hidden, seeks what is concealed, and in the swift ravaging of its flames it seizes whatever has destroyed erring men with vain persuasions. For "the day of the Lord," it says, "comes like a burning oven." You have heard what is coming. There is nothing gathered from you that can be laid up in the Lord's storehouses: you will burn like stubble, whose empty worthlessness is kept only for ashes and embers, on which the ravenous fire feeds as the force of the wind drives it.

This is your outcome and your end; this is the punishment God has decreed for the deceivers of men: that whoever, against the will of God, has either deceived or ruined wretched man shall burn in everlasting flames. I would like indeed to inquire carefully which Minerva they mean this image to represent. For it is agreed that there were several Minervas, and no one disagrees on this point. Let us therefore describe the particular lineage, character, skill and pursuit of each, so that from all of these it may be found in the name of which Minerva the Palladium was consecrated.

Antiquity hands down to us, as we read, that there were five Minervas. One is the daughter of Vulcan, who founded Athens, and whom a rustic throng accompanied from the countryside into the order of city life. Another was in Egypt, daughter of King Nile, a mistress of the weaving art. The third was born of Saturn as her father, but they record that she was a manlike woman: for she never kept herself within the modesty of the female sex, but always pursued arms and the din of battle and the bloody business of war. The fourth was the daughter of Jupiter, king of Crete, who reported to her father that Liber had been slain. The fifth was born of Pallas as her father and

a Titaness as her mother, and was called Pallas by men, named after her father. Driven by parricidal madness and urged on by insane recklessness, she butchered her father Pallas with a cruel death; and not content with her father's simple death, so that she might enjoy her wickedness longer and triumph more cruelly over her father's death, [she adorned herself] with the spoils of his body [?], so as to publish the crime of parricide by a cruel display. It is in the name of this woman—oh, the outrage!—that the Palladium is consecrated; this is the Pallas who is worshipped, this is the one preserved by pontifical law; and she whose crime ought to have been condemned more severely is the one whose image is humbly adored. Set fire to it, feed the flames, so that by your daily sacrifices she may learn to burn. For what else does a parricide deserve than to be burned every day in avenging flames, in a perpetual foreshadowing of the fire, before the sentence of God?

These, most sacred emperors, should be called tombs, not temples; rather they should be called the pyres of wretched men. For the pitiable servitude of men builds shrines in place of sepulchres in honour of lost men. Here the embers of cremated bodies are kept; here the ashes of the dead are laid away by an irreligious law, so that the misfortunes of bitter deaths may break open afresh with the daily blood of victims, so that the end that brought sad lamentation may be renewed and reborn in annual mourning, so that fresh wailing may stir up tears long laid to rest, so that from the rites of these sacred things the wretched mind of man may learn both to worship and to commit parricides, incests and murders.

These things, most sacred emperors, must be cut away and utterly destroyed, and corrected by the most severe laws of your edicts, so that the deadly error of this presumption may no longer stain the Roman world, so that the wickedness of a pestilent custom may not grow strong, so that whatever tries to destroy the man of God may no longer hold sway on earth. Some are unwilling and resist, and long for their own destruction with headlong desire; but come to the aid of the wretched, free those who are perishing. It is for this that the supreme God has entrusted the empire to you, that through you the wound of this plague may be healed. We know the danger of their crime; the penalties of their error are well known; but it is better that you free them against their will than that you grant them destruction because they want it.

The sick delight in what is harmful, and when ill health has taken hold of a person's body, the sufferers demand perverse things contrary to their own recovery. The mind, captured by the vice of weakness, always craves what will worsen the disease; it spurns and despises the remedies of the skilled, rejects the cure of medicine, and hurries with headlong eagerness toward its own destruction. Then, if the evil of the disease grows stronger, stronger remedies are sought, and medicine, anxious for the patient's recovery, arms itself more vigorously: harsh foods and bitter drinks are forced on the unwilling, and if the illness gains strength, fire and the knife are applied as well. So a man, once his health is recovered and his well-being restored to him, acknowledges with a settled mind that everything he suffered against his will because of his sick body was all done for his own good.

Hear now, most holy princes, also the reasoning by which their names were composed. This light, which by the command of God drives away the darkness and gives men back the day, and which directs the order of its course through the span of twelve hours, they chose to call Sol, the Sun—not because it is alone (solus), as some would have it (for in the sky there is also the moon and very many other stars that we see, some of which shine in a single row, joined together in perpetual coherence, while others, scattered over the whole sky, measure out wandering courses in their own erratic paths), but it is called Sol because, when it has risen, it alone (solus) shines, the other stars being darkened.

Luna, the Moon—who is also Lucina—took her name from her light (lumen) by night. Some also chose to call her Diana, because by shining through the night she makes for men almost a second day (dies). Those who swim the sea chose to call it Neptune, from swimming (natare), shaping the substance of the name from what they liked to do. The whole power and nature of the earth they call Father Dis, because it is the nature of the earth that all things fall back into it and, having arisen from it, come forth again—a fact that displayed the opulence and riches (divitiae) of the earth.

The substance of the crops they want to call Proserpina, because crops, once they begin to be sown, are of profit (prosunt) to men. The earth itself they name Ceres, borrowing this name from bearing (gerere) fruits. Mavors took his name from the fortunes of war, as if he "overturns great things" (magna vertat). Minerva likewise is a warlike name, as though she either diminishes (minuat) or threatens (minetur). The comeliness (venustas) of men was called Venus. The name of Apollo they invented in the Greek tongue from human misfortunes, as though he either loses or destroys everything entrusted to him. Some also call the sun Apollo, because every day, when it sets, it loses the brightness of its light; and the Greeks call "to lose" apollyein. You see how turbulent error has devised your false and fictitious

gods, so that both the forms and the names of the gods have been handed down to you through old wives' superstitions. But truth has uncovered all these things, and the reason of a sound mind has found them out, so that once everything that sacrilegious error had hidden was investigated and exposed, truth might shine in life. For when all these things had been wickedly contrived, at first they terrified mortals; then, when their novelty had worn off, as men recovered as if from a long illness, a kind of contempt was born out of their wonder. So little by little the mind dared to inquire carefully into what had stupefied it, and at once it turned its keen intelligence on the secrets of these fictitious and empty superstitions. Then, gathering the explanation of hidden things through constant study, it arrived at their causes, so that the human race first learned the pitiable inventions of profane religions, then despised them, and thirdly rejected them.

I now wish to explain by what signs or by what passwords the wretched crowd of men recognize one another in these very superstitions. For they have their own signs, their own responses, which the teaching of the devil has handed down to them in the gatherings of these sacrileges. In a certain temple, so that the man who is about to enter may be admitted to the inner parts, he says: "I have eaten from the drum, I have drunk from the cymbal, and I have learned the secrets of the religion"—which in the Greek tongue is said: "From the drum I have eaten, from the cymbal I have drunk, I have become an initiate of Attis."

Wretched man, you do ill to confess the crime you have committed: you have drained the pestilent venom of poison, and at the prompting of an unholy frenzy you have licked up a deadly cup. Death and punishment always follow that food; what you boast of having drunk binds the vein of life to death, defiles the seat of the soul, and throws it into turmoil with an unbroken succession of evils. There is another food, which bestows salvation and life; there is another food, which both commends man to the supreme God and restores him to him; there is another food, which lifts up the faint, calls back the wandering, raises the fallen, and bestows on the dying the marks of eternal immortality. Seek the bread of Christ, the cup of Christ, so that, scorning earthly frailty, the substance of man may be fed on immortal nourishment.

But what is this bread, or what cup, that Wisdom proclaims with a loud voice in the books of Solomon? For she says, "Come, eat of my bread and drink the wine I have mixed for you." And Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the most high God, offered Abraham on his return the grace of blessing with bread and wine. Isaac too, when he had blessed Jacob and Esau humbly begged the same of his father, answered him: "I have made him your lord, and I have made all his brothers his servants; with wheat and wine I have established him." Then Esau bewailed his lot in wretched lamentation, because he had lost the grace of wheat and wine, that is, of future happiness.

That this divine bread is granted by God to those consecrated to him, the Holy Spirit says through Isaiah: "Thus says the Lord: Behold, those who serve me shall eat, but you shall be hungry; behold, those who serve me shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame; the Lord will slay you." Not only is this bread denied by the supreme God to the sacrilegious and impious, but punishment is promised as well, and the destruction of a bitter death is decreed, so that the ruin of divine punishment may be thrust into their hungry jaws.

The venerable words of the thirty-third psalm also follow the same thought, for the Holy Spirit says through David: "Taste and see that the Lord is sweet." Sweet is the heavenly nourishment, sweet the food of God: it holds no grim torment of wretched hunger, and it drives out from the marrow of men the venom of poison that spreads from within. That this is so the following words of the oracle declare, for it says: "Fear the Lord, you his holy ones, for there is no want for those who fear him. The rich have been in need and gone hungry, but those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing."

You who walk thus in the temple in your bordered toga, who gleam in purple, whose head is weighed down with gold or laurel—shameful want follows your error, and the heavy burden of poverty hangs over your neck. The poor man whom you despise is bountiful and rich; Abraham is preparing a seat for him in his bosom. Then you, across the intervening expanse of flames, will beg from him a tiny drop of trickling water to soothe the wounds of your conscience, and Lazarus, though willing, will be able neither to give nor to obtain for you any relief from your pain. For the deserts of each are weighed with equal justice: life is conferred on him because of the evils of this world, while on you the everlasting punishment of torments is decreed because of the good things of this world.

And so that it might be learned more clearly what that bread is through which the destruction of wretched death is overcome, the Lord himself declared it with his holy and venerable mouth, lest the hope of men be deceived by perverse interpretations in various treatises. For he says in the Gospel according to John: "I am the bread of life: whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst." Again, in what follows, he signifies the same in a similar way, for he says: "If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink, whoever believes in me." And again he himself, to impart to believers the substance of his majesty, says: "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink

his blood, you will not have life in you." Therefore, wretched mortals, have nothing to do with the food of the drum: seek the grace of the saving food and drink the immortal cup. Christ calls you back to the light by his banquet, and gives life to limbs rotting [?] with grievous poison and to numbed members. Renew the lost man with heavenly food, so that whatever in you is dead may be reborn through the divine gifts. You have learned what you ought to do; choose what you will: from the one, death is born; by the other, immortal life is granted.

[?] "Hail, bridegroom, hail, new light." Why do you hurl wretched man down the precipice like this, you ruinous persuasion? Why do you promise him the trappings of a false hope? There is no light with you, nor is there anyone there who deserves to be hailed as bridegroom. There is one light, there is one bridegroom: Christ has received the grace of these names. You will not be able to transfer to yourself the glory of another's happiness, nor be adorned with the splendour of heavenly light. You have been cast out into darkness and squalor: there filth, squalor, gloom and darkness reign, and the horror of everlasting night.

If you want even a faint gleam of light to shine on you, lift up your face, open your sunken eyes, and, abandoning these things, betake yourself to him who said, "I am the light of the world," whose divine commandments contain the precept that in this earthly life our work should shine day by day. But it cannot shine unless the adornments of a spotless conscience protect us, unless a whole and uncorrupted life commends us. Then the grace of the true light will rise upon us, then the author of light makes his way into us, then we can both receive and see the true light.

But to check the insolence of that sacrilegious cry, I shall prove from the oracles of the sacred readings who is truly the bridegroom, so that it may be proved that the bridegroom is Christ and the bride the Church, from whom spiritual sons are born day by day to the venerable Father. In this proof let the venerable secrets of the prophets be laid open; let the faithfulness of the holy oracles stand by us. Joel, moved by the divine Spirit, says: "Blow the trumpet in Zion, sanctify a fast and proclaim a healing, gather the people, sanctify the assembly, receive the elders, gather the little ones at the breast; let the bridegroom come forth from his chamber and the bride from her bridal room."

Jeremiah signifies the same in a similar way, for he says, when he threatens Jerusalem with a fierce oracle: "And I will take away from the cities of Judah and from the crossroads of Jerusalem the voice of those who rejoice, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride." The Holy Spirit also proclaims the coming forth of the bridegroom through the psalms; in the eighteenth psalm this oracle is found, for it says: "And he, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber, will exult like a giant to run his course;

his going forth is from the height of heaven, and his circuit runs to its height again, and there is none who can hide from his heat." Let more hidden secrets be laid open: in the Apocalypse we find who the bridegroom is. For thus it is written: "Come, I will show you the new bride, the wife of the Lamb. And he carried me away in the spirit to a great mountain and showed me the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven." We must also set forth what the teaching of the Gospel hands down to us on this very matter. For we find it recorded thus in the Gospel according to John: "You are my witnesses that I said to those who were sent to me from Jerusalem that I am not the Christ, but that I have been sent before him. For he who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice."

The mystery of this has been revealed; the choir of wise virgins awaits the coming of this bridegroom; for him holy virginity holds up lamps with watchful care; to the servants who await the bridegroom the gift of blessed rewards is promised. For we find in the Gospel according to Luke: "Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning, and be like men waiting for their master to come back from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks they may open to him. Blessed are those servants whom the master finds watching when he comes." See, by the oracles of venerable responses the bridegroom has been revealed.

Why do you, set amid bitter misfortunes, give yourself a blessed name? If you wish to be set free and follow the light of the bridegroom, cast off your errors and, anxious and watchful, chastise the crimes of your past life with religious devotion. Then, when the bridegroom finds you watching in his name, when he recognizes the merits of your faith, he will give you the greatest reward, he will give you a perfect gift: you will enter with him the bridal chamber of heaven, you will see the palace of the world, and, so that you may be a true partaker, the grace of immortality will be conferred on you by the most loving and most just Lord.

The token of another profane rite is θεὸς ἐκ πέτρας, "god from the rock." Why do you take this holy and venerable mystery, falsify what it professes, and carry it over to profane acts? There is another stone, which God promised he would lay when he made firm the foundations of the promised Jerusalem: Christ is shown to us under the figure of that venerable stone. Why do you, with stealthy fraud, carry the dignity of that venerable name over to your defiled superstitions? Your stone is followed by ruin and by the deadly collapse of falling roofs. Our stone, laid by the hand of God, builds up, strengthens, raises, fortifies, and adorns the grace of the restored work with the splendor of everlasting immortality. For Isaiah, at the bidding of the Holy Spirit, says of it:

"Thus says the Lord: Behold, I lay in the foundations of Zion a precious stone, chosen, the chief cornerstone, held in honor; and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame." In the Psalms too a similar answer is given, for the Holy Spirit says in the hundred and seventeenth Psalm: "The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner; this was done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes." Through a great many prophets the Holy Spirit makes known the meaning of this name, for the prophet Zechariah says: "Behold, I bring my servant; Rising is his name; for the stone that I have set before the face of Jesus: upon that one stone are seven eyes."

But to make this plainer still, let us lay open the more ancient mysteries of the sacred readings. In Deuteronomy it is set down thus: "And you shall write all this law upon a stone." Joshua the son of Nun too, at God's command, set this down expressly, for it says: "And he took a great stone and set it up before the Lord. And Joshua said to the people: Behold, this stone shall be a witness for me, for it has heard all the things that were spoken by the Lord when he spoke to you; and it shall be a witness to you in the last of days, when

you have turned away from your Lord." And that through this stone, that is, through our Lord Jesus Christ, these gods of yours are to fall, together with the whole multitude of temples, Daniel has openly declared in his venerable oracles, for when he was interpreting the king's dream he said: "And behold, an image, an exceedingly great image, and the sight of that image was fearful, and it stood raised up before you. Its head was of fine gold, its breast and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze, and its feet partly of iron and partly of clay, until a stone was cut out of a mountain without the hands of cutters, and it struck the image upon its feet of iron and clay and broke them in pieces; and the iron and the clay, the bronze, the silver and the gold were broken together and became like chaff, like the dust on a threshing floor in summer, and the wind carried them away, so that nothing of them remained; and the stone that struck the image became a great mountain and filled

the whole earth." What place on earth is there that the name of Christ has not taken possession of? Where the sun rises and where it sets, where the north lifts itself up and where the south slopes down, the majesty of the venerable Godhead will fill it all. And though in some regions the dying limbs of idolatry still twitch, things have nevertheless reached the point where this pestilent evil is about to be cut out root and branch from all Christian lands. As for the stone of the idolaters, of which they say "god from the rock" [?], what answer has the oracle of the prophets given about it? And whom has this stone ever withstood, or whom does it spare?

But this holy stone, that is, Christ, either upholds the foundations of faith [?], or, set at the corner, joins the members of two walls in balanced measure, that is, gathers into one the nations of the Old and the New Testament; or indeed unites the diversity of body and soul [?] in man with immortality; or promulgates the law; or bears witness against sinners; or, what is more, strikes the image of the devil, so that when he has been overcome and laid low and turned to ash and cinders, the pure rule of his dominion may stand, with the summit of his majesty raised on high.

Now, most sacred Emperors Constantius and Constans, the power of your venerable faith must also be called upon: that faith which is lifted above men and set apart from earthly frailty, which joins itself in fellowship with heavenly things, which in all its acts follows, as far as it can, the will of the most high God. Only a little remains before the devil lies utterly laid low by your laws, and the deadly contagion of extinguished idolatry perishes. The venom of this poison has faded away, and day by day the substance of profane desire is breathing its last. Raise the banner of faith; God has reserved this for you. By his favor you have become eminent as the vanquishers of all your enemies, through whose doings the Roman Empire was being weakened. Raise the standard of the venerable law; decree and promulgate what will be of benefit. May it be auspicious and happy for the state that amid heaps of slaughtered victims you have laid low the army of the enemy. Happy are you too: God has made you sharers in his glory and his will; Christ in his favor has reserved for his people, by your hands, the destruction of idolatry and the overthrow of the profane temples. He conquered the evil spirits with spiritual weapons; you have conquered the evils of the earth. Raise the trophies of victory and let a great inscription of your triumphs be carried before you. Rejoicing in the overthrow of profane things, exult more boldly, exult with confidence. Your good fortune is joined to the power of God; with Christ fighting for the salvation of mankind, you have conquered.

Let all the tokens of the profane religion be set out in order, so that we may prove that the most wicked enemy of the human race has taken these things from the holy and venerable oracles of the prophets and carried them over to the polluted crimes of his madness.

For we find it said thus: εὐοῖ, δίκερως δίμορφε, "Euhoi, two-horned, two-formed one!" This god of yours is not two-formed but many-formed, for the shape of that venomous mouth changes into many guises. He is the basilisk and the scorpion that is trodden under the untroubled feet of the faithful; he is the malicious serpent whose head deceived mankind seeks to crush; he is the twisting dragon who is led by a hook and shut up as a captive. This god of yours is adorned with the locks of the Lernaean serpent. Do you see how, when the master is struck, a crowd of dying snakes takes his place? Why do you sprout like this, with hydras forever being reborn? Why do you deck yourself out with a fertile brood of crimes?

We have learned the way to your death; we know the remedies by which the poisons of your art are overcome. We drink the immortal blood of Christ; the blood of Christ has been joined to our blood. This is the saving remedy against your crimes; this daily drives the deadly poison out of the corrupted people of God. Who has ever seen this god they mourn with horns? What are these horns he boasts of having? There are other horns, which the prophet records at the bidding of the Holy Spirit, and which you, devil, imagine you can transfer to your own defiled face.

Why do you seek ornaments and glory for yourself from that source? The horns show nothing other than the venerable sign of the cross. By one arm of this sign, stretched out straight, the world is upheld and the earth held together; and by the joining of the two arms that go out to the sides the east is touched and the west lifted up, so that the whole world is made firm by a threefold stability, and the foundations of the work, fixed in place, are held by immortal roots. This mystery the venerable oracle of the prophet has handed down to us, for we find it written thus in Habakkuk: "His power has covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise, and his splendor shall be as the light; horns shall be in his hands, and there the power of his glory has been established, and he has set his love; the Word shall go forth and go before him at his steps."

Behold the venerable horns of the cross; behold the immortal summit of holy power; behold the divine framework of a glorious work! You, Christ, with outstretched hands uphold the world and the earth; you uphold the heavenly kingdom; our salvation clings to your immortal shoulders; you, Lord, carry the sign of eternal life; you by your venerable inspiration announce this to us through the prophets. For Isaiah says: "Behold, a son is born to us; the government is upon his shoulders, and his name is called Messenger of Great Counsel." These are the horns of the cross, by which all things are both lifted up and held together alike; by these horns human life is well served. That Amalek might be conquered, Moses imitated these horns with outstretched hands; that he might more easily obtain what he earnestly prayed for, he made himself a cross out of a rod. Hurry with all speed to these horns; take refuge in these horns with humble reverence. May justice, fairness, chastity, mercy, patience and faith fasten you to these horns, so that, bearing these venerable insignia before you and rejoicing in the majesty of a consecrated brow, you may be sharers both in Christ's burial and in his life.

We bring forward yet another token, so that the crimes of polluted thinking may be exposed. Its whole procedure must be described, so that it may be clear to all that the law of the divine plan has been corrupted by the devil's perverse imitation. On a certain night an image is laid on its back on a litter and is mourned with laments arranged in measured order. Then, when they have had their fill of feigned lamentation, a light is brought in. Then the priest anoints the throats of all who were weeping, and when they have been anointed, the priest whispers this in a slow murmur: θαρρεῖτε μύσται τοῦ θεοῦ σεσωσμένου· ἔσται γὰρ ἡμῖν ἐκ πόνων σωτηρία, "Take heart, initiates, since the god has been saved; for we too shall have salvation from our toils." Why do you urge these wretches to rejoice?

Why do you drive deceived people to be glad? What hope, what salvation do you promise them with your deadly persuasion? Why do you entice them with a false promise? The death of your god is known; his life is nowhere to be seen. No divine oracle ever spoke of his resurrection, nor did he show himself to men after death so that he might be believed; he gave no proofs of such a deed beforehand, nor did he show by earlier examples that he would do it. You bury an idol;

you mourn an idol; you bring an idol out of its tomb; and, wretch that you are, when you have done these things you rejoice. You set your god free; you arrange the limbs of a stone lying on the ground; you set upright an insensible rock. Let your god give you thanks, let him repay you with equal gifts, let him make you his partner: may you die as he dies and live as he lives.

As for their throats being anointed with perfume, who would not see through the emptiness of that deed and despise it? So the devil has his own christs, his own anointed ones, and since he himself is the antichrist, he draws wretched people into a criminal fellowship, to the disgrace of his own name. Keep this ointment for the dead, keep it for those about to die, so that those you have caught in your snares, once smeared with poisoned ointment, you may forever plunge into mournful and deadly ruin.

There is another ointment, which God the Father gave to his only Son, and which the Son bestows on believers by the divine majesty of his Godhead. Christ's ointment is made of an immortal compound and blended with the spiritual fragrances of spices. This ointment strips the decaying limbs of men free of the snares of death, so that when the first man has been buried, at once another man is born more happily out of that same man. And to explain this more plainly, the secrets of the sacred readings must be laid open.
